title: CMLRE Unveils Landmark National Report on Deep-Sea and Distant-Water Fishery Resources of the Indian EEZ to Fuel Sustainable Blue Economy
body_text:
NEW DELHI — As global focus intensifies on ocean-driven food security and climate regulation, India has taken a definitive step toward mapping and managing its vast, uncharted marine frontiers. Marking the Silver Jubilee celebrations of the Centre for Marine Living Resources & Ecology (CMLRE), the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES) has released the comprehensive “National Report on Deep-Sea and Distant-Water Fishery Resources of the Indian EEZ.”
The milestone document compiles nearly four decades of pioneering oceanographic research and three decades of systematic surveys across India's 2.37 million square kilometre Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). Far more than a scientific archive, the report delivers a definitive roadmap for the sustainable development of India’s Blue Economy, balancing resource assessment with biodiversity conservation.
The report was formally unveiled in the presence of Dr. M. Ravichandran , Former Secretary, MoES, alongside former CMLRE Directors Dr. P. Madheswaran and Dr. M. Sudhakar; Dr. M. V. Ramana Murthy, Director of the Deep Ocean Mission; and Dr. R. S. Maheskumar, Head of CMLRE, alongside senior members of the marine science community.
Decades of Exploration Aboard a Floating Laboratory
The findings presented in the report represent an unprecedented collective scientific effort, encompassing more than 400 oceanographic cruises since the early 1990s under the Marine Living Resources Programme (MLRP). At the heart of this massive endeavor is India’s flagship research vessel, the Fishery and Oceanographic Research Vessel (FORV) Sagar Sampada .
Serving as a sophisticated floating laboratory, the vessel carried multidisciplinary teams of scientists through grueling, weeks-long expeditions across the Arabian Sea, the Bay of Bengal, the Lakshadweep waters, the Andaman Sea, and into the Southern Ocean (Antarctica) to map species distributions, estimate fish abundance, and capture critical environmental data.
Key Highlights from the Deep-Sea Frontier
Unlocking the "Twilight Zone" (Mesopelagic Layer): Extending from 200 to 1,000 meters deep, this zone houses dense communities of lanternfishes (myctophids), deep-sea shrimps, and cephalopods. The report details how their nightly vertical migration drives the ocean's "biological carbon pump," transferring carbon from the surface to the deep sea to regulate global climate. Deep-Sea Demersal Resources: The report provides a meticulous assessment of living resources inhabiting the continental slope beyond 200 meters, identifying substantial, currently underexploited stocks of deep-sea shrimps, perches, scombroids, flatfishes, and eels. Distant-Water Fisheries: Comprehensive data is compiled on high-value open-ocean and deep-water species, including tunas, billfishes, sharks, oceanic squids, and Antarctic krill. Safeguarding Marine Biodiversity Hotspots: Crucially, the publication documents ecologically vital regions that serve as nurseries and habitats for vulnerable ecosystems. Key areas highlighted include: Kollam Bank & Angria Bank Off-Mangalore Deep-Sea Slope Terrace off Trivandrum The Lakshadweep and Andaman-Nicobar Islands
A Tech-Driven Vision for 2047
The report highlights how modern, emerging technologies are transforming Indian oceanography. By integrating historical field observations with fisheries acoustics, environmental DNA (eDNA), autonomous observing platforms, satellite observations, artificial intelligence (AI), and advanced ecosystem modelling , India is establishing a state-of-the-art framework for marine spatial planning.
This scientific foundation directly reinforces India's Vision 2047 , which prioritises the Blue Economy as a core pillar of national growth. It also strengthens India's global commitments to UN Sustainable Development Goal 14 (Life Below Water) and the UN Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development.
"Sustainable prosperity will not come simply from discovering new marine resources, but from understanding them, respecting the ecosystems that sustain them, and managing them with science as the guiding compass," said Dr M Ravichandran.
The publication was edited by Dr V. N. Sanjeevan (former Director, CMLRE) and Dr Baban Ingole (retired Scientist, NIO Goa), and published under the leadership of Dr R. S. Maheskumar . The core authorial team responsible for synthesising this massive repository of multi-disciplinary data includes Dr Hashim Manjebrayakath, Dr Smitha B. R., Dr Rajeesh Kumar M. P., Dr Meera K. M., Dr Purbali Saha, Dr Sahina Akter, Dr Chinmay Kar, and Dr Davood Nihal.
Picture: Former Secretary, Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES), Dr. M. Ravichandran,  released the National Report on Deep-Sea and Distant-Water Fishery Resources of Indian EEZ during the Silver Jubilee celebrations of the Centre for Marine Living Resources & Ecology (CMLRE), Kochi, in the presence of former Directors, senior scientists, Head of CMLRE, authors, and distinguished members of the marine science community.
*****
NKR/JKP

enrichment.summary: To mark the Silver Jubilee of the Centre for Marine Living Resources & Ecology (CMLRE), the Ministry of Earth Sciences released the 'National Report on Deep-Sea and Distant-Water Fishery Resources of the Indian EEZ.' The report synthesises nearly four decades of oceanographic research and over 400 research cruises since the early 1990s, largely aboard the FORV Sagar Sampada, covering India's 2.37 million sq km Exclusive Economic Zone. It assesses underexploited deep-sea and distant-water fishery resources (mesopelagic species, deep-sea demersal stocks, tunas, billfishes, Antarctic krill), identifies key marine biodiversity hotspots, and proposes a technology-driven roadmap using AI, eDNA and acoustics for marine spatial planning under India's Blue Economy vision.
enrichment.context:
India's EEZ remains vastly underexplored compared to its coastal fisheries, which are already near or beyond sustainable exploitation limits. The Marine Living Resources Programme (MLRP), run through CMLRE (an autonomous institute under MoES based in Kochi) and its research vessel FORV Sagar Sampada, was established precisely to survey these deeper, less-accessible resources so that India can diversify fishing effort away from overstressed coastal waters toward deep-sea and distant-water fisheries. This report is significant because it consolidates decades of survey data into an actionable resource assessment, highlighting substantial stocks of deep-sea shrimp, perches and cephalopods, as well as ecologically sensitive habitats like the Kollam Bank and Angria Bank that need protective management even as exploitation is scaled up.

The release also ties into India's broader Blue Economy policy architecture, including the Deep Ocean Mission (a mission for exploring deep-sea resources, biodiversity and technologies), and international commitments such as UN SDG 14 (Life Below Water) and the UN Decade of Ocean Science. The mesopelagic 'twilight zone' findings are particularly relevant to climate science, as the vertical migration of species like lanternfish is central to the ocean's biological carbon pump — a natural process of carbon sequestration increasingly discussed in climate mitigation debates. For India, moving fishing effort into the mesopelagic and demersal deep-sea zones responsibly, rather than depleting them as has happened with surface fisheries elsewhere, is framed as central to Vision 2047's blue growth pillar.

prelims_questions.question: The 'biological carbon pump' referred to in the context of deep-sea mesopelagic organisms primarily involves which process?
options: Absorption of atmospheric carbon dioxide directly by ocean surface currents
Vertical migration of organisms like lanternfish transferring carbon from surface to deep ocean layers
Chemical weathering of oceanic rocks trapping carbon dioxide
Coral reef calcification storing carbon in reef structures
prelims_questions.explanation: The release explains that the nightly vertical migration of mesopelagic species such as lanternfish (myctophids) drives the ocean's biological carbon pump by transferring carbon from the surface to deep-sea layers, helping regulate global climate.

prelims_questions.question: Which research vessel has served as India's primary platform for surveys under the Marine Living Resources Programme (MLRP) referenced in the CMLRE national report?
prelims_questions.explanation: The report notes that FORV Sagar Sampada, described as a floating laboratory, conducted over 400 oceanographic cruises since the early 1990s under the MLRP across Indian waters and the Southern Ocean.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the significance of deep-sea and distant-water fishery resources for India's Blue Economy. What scientific and institutional mechanisms exist to ensure their sustainable exploitation?
Examine the ecological role of the mesopelagic 'twilight zone' in regulating global climate and the challenges of balancing its resource potential with biodiversity conservation.

study_notes.reason: The release carries a solid factual core (CMLRE, FORV Sagar Sampada, EEZ dimensions, Deep Ocean Mission, mesopelagic zone definition) that UPSC could test directly, while also offering substantial analytical material on blue economy strategy, sustainable resource diversification and climate linkages via the biological carbon pump — neither side clearly dominates.

prelims.point: CMLRE (Centre for Marine Living Resources & Ecology) is an autonomous institute under the Ministry of Earth Sciences, based in Kochi, that runs the Marine Living Resources Programme (MLRP).
prelims.why_important: Institution-ministry pairing and its programme mandate is a classic matching-type prelims item.

prelims.point: FORV Sagar Sampada is India's Fishery and Oceanographic Research Vessel used for over 400 cruises since the early 1990s to survey the EEZ.
prelims.why_important: Vessel names tied to specific missions are frequently used as distractors in prelims questions on India's ocean research infrastructure.

prelims.point: India's Exclusive Economic Zone covers about 2.37 million sq km.
prelims.why_important: A specific numerical fact on India's maritime jurisdiction that could appear in a statement-based question.

prelims.point: The Deep Ocean Mission is a Ministry of Earth Sciences initiative for exploring deep-sea resources, biodiversity and technologies, referenced here through its Director.
prelims.why_important: A flagship mission often tested for its parent ministry and core objectives, distinguishing it from other ocean-related schemes.

mains.point: India's coastal fisheries are near or beyond sustainable limits, making diversification of fishing effort toward deep-sea and distant-water resources central to sustainable Blue Economy growth.
mains.analytical_use: Useful for questions on sustainable exploitation of marine resources or India's Blue Economy strategy under Vision 2047.

mains.point: The report proposes integrating AI, eDNA, acoustics, satellite observation and ecosystem modelling for marine spatial planning.
mains.analytical_use: Can be used to discuss how emerging technologies are transforming resource assessment and governance in the maritime/environment sector.

mains.point: The report identifies ecologically sensitive biodiversity hotspots (e.g., Kollam Bank, Angria Bank) that must be protected even as deep-sea exploitation is scaled up, highlighting the exploitation-conservation trade-off.
mains.analytical_use: Relevant for questions on balancing economic exploitation of marine resources with ecological conservation.

both.concept: The mesopelagic 'twilight zone' (200–1000 m depth) hosts lanternfish and other species whose nightly vertical migration drives the ocean's biological carbon pump, a natural carbon sequestration process.
both.prelims_angle: Could be tested as a factual definition: depth range of the mesopelagic zone, key species (myctophids), and the term 'biological carbon pump'.
both.mains_angle: Provides material for analysing the ocean's role in climate regulation and how responsible exploitation of this zone must consider its climate function, tying fisheries policy to climate mitigation debates.

low_priority.point: List of officials and scientists present at the report's unveiling ceremony.
low_priority.reason: Ceremonial detail with no factual or analytical exam value.

low_priority.point: Names of editors and authorial team who compiled the report.
low_priority.reason: Administrative attribution detail, not testable or analytically relevant.

related_articles.title: PARLIAMENT QUESTION: ADVANCED MARINE STATION FOR OCEAN BIOLOGY
related_articles.relationship: This Parliament reply detailed CMLRE's ongoing EEZ surveys (19 surveys during 2023-2026) for fishery resource and marine biodiversity assessment, which is the same institutional research program that culminated in this new national report on deep-sea and distant-water fishery resources.
